page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question
Chemical Equilibrium, Acids and Bases · 2 marks

steps.label: The definition
lines: Salt hydrolysis is the reaction between the
cation or the anion (or both) of a dissolved
salt and water, giving an acidic, basic or
It is the reverse of neutralisation.
steps.why: A salt has no H⁺ or OH⁻ of its own, so its solution can turn acidic or basic only if one of its ions reacts with water — that reaction is what the definition names. Not every ion does it: only the cation left by a WEAK base and the anion left by a WEAK acid react with water. The ions of strong acids and strong bases, such as Na⁺, K⁺, Cl⁻ and NO₃⁻, do not, which is why a sodium chloride solution stays neutral — that is the ABSENCE of hydrolysis, not one of its outcomes. The neutral case the definition names is the salt of a weak acid and a weak base, such as ammonium acetate, where both ions react with water to about the same extent and the two effects balance.
common_mistakes: Writing that the salt simply dissolves in water. Hydrolysis is a reaction of the ions WITH water, not dissolution.
Calling a neutral NaCl solution a case of hydrolysis. A salt of a strong acid and a strong base does not hydrolyse at all; its solution stays neutral because neither ion reacts with water.
steps.memory_tip: Hydro + lysis = splitting by water. The ion reacts with water and splits it.
steps.margin_note: Name the cation and the anion — hydrolysis is an ion-water reaction.

steps.label: The ion-water equations
lines: so a sodium acetate solution is basic.
steps.why: The two general equations show the mechanism: a cation releases H⁺ from water (acidic solution), an anion takes H⁺ from water and releases OH⁻ (basic solution). Read M⁺ and A⁻ with the condition attached: M⁺ stands for the cation of a WEAK base and A⁻ for the anion of a WEAK acid. Only those two hydrolyse. Taken without that condition the pair of equations would say every cation and every anion hydrolyses, which would make NaCl acidic and basic at once and would leave no neutral case at all — yet the definition in step 1 names a neutral case. The example given, CH₃COO⁻, is the anion of the weak acid CH₃COOH, which is exactly why it works.
common_mistakes: Writing the equations with a one-way arrow. Hydrolysis is an equilibrium, so the arrow is ⇌.
Swapping the results — cation hydrolysis gives an acidic solution, anion hydrolysis gives a basic one.
Applying the two general equations to every ion. M⁺ means the cation of a weak base and A⁻ the anion of a weak acid; Na⁺, K⁺, Cl⁻ and NO₃⁻ do not hydrolyse, so a NaCl solution is neutral.
steps.memory_tip: Cation makes the solution aCidic, Anion makes it Alkaline (basic).
steps.margin_note: Both general equations with ⇌ complete the answer. Say that M⁺ is from a weak base and A⁻ from a weak acid, then give the real example.

insider_note: Write the two ion-water equations with ⇌; the definition alone is only half the answer. Then say which ions actually hydrolyse — the cation of a weak base and the anion of a weak acid. Without that condition the general equations claim that every salt is both acidic and basic, and the neutral case in the definition disappears.
